variants.title: Design from the decision
variants.context: A composite starts from the decision, not the task list. Bound the decision, map the required capabilities, choose evidence with known provenance, then freeze the interpretation policy before any candidate is scored.
variants.prompt: A team is asked to compare two text models for multilingual support triage. Put the design steps in order.

items.text: Choose evidence: select tasks with known provenance, scoring validity, enough cases, and limited redundancy, recording gaps.
Bound the decision: name the behavior, users, languages, modality, environment, and the release action the evidence supports.
Freeze interpretation: predeclare normalization, weights, hard floors, uncertainty, missing values, exclusions, and the release rule.
Map required capabilities: translate the claim into independent capabilities, critical subgroups, failure modes, and constraints.

variants.hint: Which step decides what the number is allowed to mean?
variants.explanation: Scope precedes selection, because tasks chosen before the claim is written produce evidence nobody can attach to a decision.

variants.title: Design from the decision
variants.context: A composite starts from the decision, not the task list. Bound the decision, map the required capabilities, choose evidence with known provenance, then freeze the interpretation policy before any candidate is scored.
variants.prompt: Legal adds a non-negotiable harmful-output limit to an existing composite. Put the redesign steps in order.

items.text: Choose evidence: pick safety tasks whose provenance and scoring validity can carry a hard requirement.
Freeze interpretation: place the limit outside the compensatory average as a hard floor before scoring any candidate.
Map required capabilities: add the harm categories, affected populations, and failure modes the limit is meant to cover.
Bound the decision: restate the release action now that a harmful-output limit constrains it.

variants.hint: A requirement that cannot be traded away does not belong inside the mean.
variants.explanation: Non-compensatory requirements are declared as floors in the interpretation policy, so a strong unrelated component can never cancel them.

variants.title: Design from the decision
variants.context: A composite starts from the decision, not the task list. Bound the decision, map the required capabilities, choose evidence with known provenance, then freeze the interpretation policy before any candidate is scored.
variants.prompt: An engineer proposes adding a popular leaderboard because competitors report it. Put the steps in order to keep the design honest.

items.text: Choose evidence: accept it only if provenance, scoring validity, case count, and redundancy against current tasks are acceptable.
Map required capabilities: check whether the leaderboard covers a capability the coverage map still lacks.
Bound the decision: state which product decision this benchmark would inform and which claims it cannot support.
Freeze interpretation: give it a declared weight and anchors before results are seen, or leave it out of the decision score.

variants.hint: Popularity is not a coverage argument.
variants.explanation: Adding a benchmark first and deciding the supported capability afterwards reverses the measurement design and invites claims the evidence cannot carry.

variants.title: Version the evaluation contract
variants.context: The evaluation contract is versioned end to end: a capability manifest pins scope, the runner stores raw item-level evidence, the composite report applies the declared policy, and the release record keeps the bounded decision.
variants.prompt: A release candidate is evaluated for the first time under a new composite. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Composite report: apply direction, scale, missing values, weights, aggregation, intervals, and sensitivity analysis.
Release record: keep passed, failed, waived, and inconclusive gates beside the rollout ceiling and rollback trigger.
Evaluation runner: store item-level outputs, references, scorer inputs, errors, latency, cost, and protocol identifiers.
Capability manifest: pin the claim, required capabilities, populations, tasks, exclusions, owners, and hard floors.

variants.hint: Each stage can only consume what the stage before it preserved.
variants.explanation: Traceability means the scalar is reproducible from versioned component results, so every stage stores what the next one needs.

variants.title: Version the evaluation contract
variants.context: The evaluation contract is versioned end to end: a capability manifest pins scope, the runner stores raw item-level evidence, the composite report applies the declared policy, and the release record keeps the bounded decision.
variants.prompt: Product weights are changed from equal capabilities to observed traffic share. Put the stages in order for the new result version.

items.text: Release record: file the new version beside the old one so both decisions remain auditable.
Capability manifest: record that the weighting policy now represents traffic share and who approved it.
Composite report: recompute the aggregate under the new weights and report rank changes against the previous policy.
Evaluation runner: reuse the retained item-level records rather than rerunning the models under a different protocol.

variants.hint: A policy change creates a new result version, not a corrected old one.
variants.explanation: Weights, anchors, and aggregation are part of the result identity, so changing them produces a new version rather than overwriting a published scalar.

variants.title: Version the evaluation contract
variants.context: The evaluation contract is versioned end to end: a capability manifest pins scope, the runner stores raw item-level evidence, the composite report applies the declared policy, and the release record keeps the bounded decision.
variants.prompt: An auditor asks why a shipped candidate outranked its rival. Put the stages in order as the evidence chain is walked forward.

items.text: Composite report: shows the normalization anchors, weights, aggregation, and the uncertainty around the gap.
Capability manifest: shows which capabilities, populations, and floors the comparison was ever meant to cover.
Release record: shows which gates passed, which were waived, and what rollout ceiling the decision carried.
Evaluation runner: supplies the raw item-level outputs and protocol identifiers behind each component score.

variants.hint: Start with what the benchmark promised, not with the number it produced.
variants.explanation: An auditable composite lets a reviewer walk from scope to raw evidence to policy to decision without reconstructing any step by hand.

variants.title: Apply the declared rule
variants.context: There is no universally correct mean. A weighted arithmetic mean lets a strong component offset a weak one, a geometric mean punishes imbalance, and a worst-case rule reports the weakest required component.
variants.prompt: The contract names a weighted arithmetic mean. Normalized components are quality 0.8 at weight 0.5, robustness 0.6 at weight 0.3, and efficiency 0.4 at weight 0.2. What is the composite score?
variants.hint: Multiply each component by its own share before adding anything.
variants.explanation: A weighted arithmetic mean sums weight times component, giving 0.40 plus 0.18 plus 0.08, so a strong quality result partly offsets weak efficiency.

mistakes.feedback: That is the unweighted average, which silently replaces the declared weights with equal shares.
That is the worst component, which is the non-compensatory rule rather than the one the contract names.

variants.title: Apply the declared rule
variants.context: There is no universally correct mean. A weighted arithmetic mean lets a strong component offset a weak one, a geometric mean punishes imbalance, and a worst-case rule reports the weakest required component.
variants.prompt: The contract names an equally weighted geometric mean over two normalized components: quality 0.9 and multilingual robustness 0.4. What is the composite score?
variants.hint: Two equally weighted components combine through their product, not their sum.
variants.explanation: The geometric mean of 0.9 and 0.4 is the square root of 0.36, so the weak component pulls the composite down harder than an average would.

mistakes.feedback: That is the arithmetic mean, which lets the strong component offset the weak one.
That is the product without taking the root, so the result is not on the component scale.

variants.title: Apply the declared rule
variants.context: There is no universally correct mean. A weighted arithmetic mean lets a strong component offset a weak one, a geometric mean punishes imbalance, and a worst-case rule reports the weakest required component.
variants.prompt: The contract names a worst-case rule over required components. Normalized results are reasoning 0.85, retrieval 0.72, and safe refusal 0.35. What score does the rule report?
variants.hint: A non-compensatory rule reports one component, not a blend.
variants.explanation: A worst-case rule reports the weakest required component, so the composite is 0.35 and no strength elsewhere can raise it.

mistakes.feedback: That is the arithmetic mean, which is exactly the compensation a worst-case rule refuses.
That is the strongest component, which reports the opposite of what the rule protects.

variants.title: Decide the composite policy
variants.context: A composite embeds policy choices. Missing components, contaminated tasks, and cohort-dependent aggregates change what the scalar means, so each case needs a predeclared rule rather than a convenient one.
variants.prompt: One candidate's safety component failed to run because of a harness error, and safety is a predeclared must-pass floor. What missing-value policy applies?
options: Renormalize the remaining weights and publish a rank based on the components both candidates completed.
Score the missing component at its baseline anchor so the candidate carries a documented penalty instead.
Block the decision score until the safety component runs, since must-pass evidence cannot be inferred.
optionFeedback: Renormalizing changes the meaning of the score and lets an easier subset look equivalent to a complete evaluation.
A baseline penalty is reasonable for compensatory components, but it converts a missing hard gate into a soft number.
Correct: blocking is the policy for must-pass evidence, because a floor cannot be satisfied by an absent measurement.
variants.hint: Ask whether the missing component was compensatory or non-negotiable.
variants.explanation: Missing-value policies are predeclared, and must-pass evidence uses block, because a hard floor cannot be satisfied by a penalty or by renormalization.

variants.title: Decide the composite policy
variants.context: A composite embeds policy choices. Missing components, contaminated tasks, and cohort-dependent aggregates change what the scalar means, so each case needs a predeclared rule rather than a convenient one.
variants.prompt: A new composite uses mean win rate against this quarter's candidate cohort. A manager wants it appended to a two-year leaderboard built from a different cohort. What is the defensible response?
options: Publish it as a new result version and require a bridge study before any cross-version ranking is claimed.
Append it with a footnote naming the cohort, since the underlying tasks and scorers did not change.
Rescale the new value to the old leaderboard's range so the historical trend line stays continuous.
optionFeedback: Correct: win rate depends on the comparison set, so splicing cohorts without a bridge study invents a trend.
A footnote does not make two differently defined numbers comparable in the same ordering.
Rescaling to match a range manufactures continuity while the aggregation semantics still differ.
variants.hint: Ask what the number was computed against, not only how it was computed.
variants.explanation: Cohort-dependent aggregates change meaning when the comparison set changes, so scores from incompatible versions are not spliced into one leaderboard.

variants.title: Decide the composite policy
variants.context: A composite embeds policy choices. Missing components, contaminated tasks, and cohort-dependent aggregates change what the scalar means, so each case needs a predeclared rule rather than a convenient one.
variants.prompt: A hashing pass flags one component task as substantially overlapping the candidate's training corpus. The task is popular and covers a capability the suite needs. What should the team do?
options: Keep it as a public regression test, exclude it from decision evidence, and record the exposure in the manifest.
Discount its contribution by the measured overlap percentage so the capability stays in the aggregate.
Keep it at full weight and rely on the other components to dilute any advantage it confers.
optionFeedback: Correct: contamination is an integrity problem, so the task stays visible as a regression signal but leaves the decision score.
A statistical discount cannot restore a holdout that is no longer independent of training.
Dilution still lets exposed items raise the decision score, and it hides the finding from anyone reading the result.
variants.hint: Can any adjustment restore independence once a holdout has leaked?
variants.explanation: Contaminated components are separated from decision evidence and their exposure is recorded, because no adjustment recreates an independent holdout.

variants.title: Map each part to its job
variants.context: A composite is built from parts with separate responsibilities. Aggregation rules, missing-value policies, and system layers each answer a different question, and confusing them is how a scalar starts hiding evidence.
variants.prompt: Match each missing-value policy to what it does to the result.

pairs.label: Block
pairs.detail: Refuses a decision score until every required component has run.

pairs.label: Score at baseline
pairs.detail: Applies a documented penalty so non-participation is never rewarded.

pairs.label: Renormalize weights
pairs.detail: Compares on shared evidence only and must publish a coverage ratio.

pairs.label: Report no rank
pairs.detail: Preserves the partial component profile until candidates have comparable evidence.

variants.hint: Ask what each policy silently assumes about the missing measurement.
variants.explanation: Each policy answers a different question, so treating missing as zero without saying so is what turns an incomplete run into a false ranking.

variants.title: Map each part to its job
variants.context: A composite is built from parts with separate responsibilities. Aggregation rules, missing-value policies, and system layers each answer a different question, and confusing them is how a scalar starts hiding evidence.
variants.prompt: Match each aggregation view to the question it answers.

pairs.label: Canonical aggregate
pairs.detail: Supports stable historical comparison under one frozen combination rule.

pairs.label: Product-weighted view
pairs.detail: Reflects observed or planned workload rather than equal capability shares.

pairs.label: Hard floors
pairs.detail: Enforces safety, legal, quality, and subgroup requirements that no strength may cancel.

pairs.label: Component profile
pairs.detail: Keeps denominators and uncertainty visible for diagnosis after the scalar is computed.

variants.hint: Several views can coexist; each exists because one number cannot answer everything.
variants.explanation: Keeping multiple views is what lets a team see why the best aggregate and the eligible candidate can be different statements.

variants.title: Map each part to its job
variants.context: A composite is built from parts with separate responsibilities. Aggregation rules, missing-value policies, and system layers each answer a different question, and confusing them is how a scalar starts hiding evidence.
variants.prompt: Match each system layer to what it owns in the scoring boundary.

pairs.label: Evaluation runner
pairs.detail: Owns model calls and the immutable item-level records behind every component.

pairs.label: Component scorers
pairs.detail: Own task-specific correctness and the diagnostics for their own task.

pairs.label: Composite layer
pairs.detail: Owns only the declared direction, scale, missing-value, and aggregation conversions.

pairs.label: Release policy
pairs.detail: Owns hard gates, evidence minimums, rollout scope, and approvals.

variants.hint: Ask which layer would have to change to alter each kind of decision.
variants.explanation: Separating the layers keeps a policy change from silently rewriting raw evidence, which is what makes a composite reproducible.
